author: Syafiq Fadli, Cheong Huei Ting
title: States refuse to act on South East Asia’s transboundary haze
content:
The recent State of Global Air report published by the Health Effects Institute and published on the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service website, identified Southeast Asia, East Asia, and Oceania as the region with the fourth-highest death rates attributable to air pollution, at 100 deaths per 100,000 people.

The World Health Organization reports that “when inhaled, health-damaging pollutants including small particulates can penetrate deep into the respiratory system and enter the bloodstream, allowing them to reach almost all organs within the body, including but not limited to cardiovascular, reproductive and metabolic systems, brain, liver and kidneys.”

The wildfires in parts of Indonesia, which started in early September, have impacted communities across South East Asia. Malaysian climate activists Syafiq Fadli and Huei Ting Cheong look at the origins of this toxic air pollution and why governments still refuse to take serious action to protect lives.

Transboundary haze has been a recurring environmental issue in Malaysia and the Southeast Asia region since the late 1990s, caused by slash-and-burn land clearing methods to cultivate palm oil plantations and a highly humid tropical climate with temperature fluctuations. It is a form of air pollution characterised by fine particles in the atmosphere that comprise pollutants such as smoke, dust, and industrial emissions, which combine with water vapour. This massive scale of air pollution has occurred so frequently it is now referred to as the “haze season”.

But this year’s haze has been extremely serious. It has been going on for about 2 months and no indication of stopping, further exacerbated by the El Niño weather system, which has brought drier conditions to the region. It is still treated as a “natural disaster”, however, ordinary people are suffering the consequences of actions by large agriculture companies, proven by countless studies and activists on the field.

Oil palms are not native to Malaysia or Indonesia, yet these two countries are at the heart of Southeast Asia’s palm oil empire, accounting for roughly 85% of global palm oil production. European colonial powers first introduced oil palms to the region as ornamental plants. However, as rubber markets declined after World War I, colonial plantation economies began shifting towards oil palm as a new profitable commodity, transforming vast stretches of land in Malaya and Indonesia into plantations.

This shift came at a devastating cost. Native plants, traditional food systems and self-sufficient ways of life were disrupted or destroyed to make way for commercial agriculture. Indigenous communities and local populations were displaced and subjected to exploitative labour systems, including indentured and contract labour, under colonial plantation regimes in the region. What was once a landscape shaped by diverse ecosystems and local livelihoods was increasingly reorganised around extraction and profit.

Today, the colonisers have left, but the plundering and destruction continues - this time by modern capitalist forces, driven by agribusinesses across Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia. Vast areas of biodiverse tropical rainforest in Malaysia and Indonesia have been cleared for palm oil plantations, contributing to severe biodiversity loss, habitat destruction and deforestation.

The fires and transboundary haze that plague the region are also linked to a complex web of corporate ownership, plantation concessions and business interests. Companies identified in reporting and investigations into plantation-related fires and land clearing include Malaysian firms and Indonesian plantation operators connected to Singapore-based business groups.

Examples include: PT Damai Agro Sejahtera — affiliated with Singapore-headquartered Bumitama Agri Ltd; and PT Arjuna Utama Sawit — identified as part of First Borneo Plantations, a plantation business with reported Singapore connections, and more.

The underlying pattern remains strikingly familiar: land and forests are treated as resources to be extracted for profit for the colonial powers back then and agribusinesses today, while indigenous communities, local livelihoods and the environment bear the consequences. When the profit is fully extracted, no compensation is given to the people, and barely any conservation efforts are made.

Such is the case with capitalism, where the world’s resources are exploited for the benefit of the few, while ordinary people are left with the consequences and the bill.

If agribusinesses are working across borders to keep businesses running as usual with no regard for people and the environment, so are the ruling classes of Indonesia and Malaysia. Indonesia’s environment minister claims the forest fire will clear up in 1 month. Malaysia's Deputy Prime Minister, Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, claims any action regarding the haze will strain Indonesia-Malaysia ties. Both are asking citizens to “be patient” and “brave this issue a little longer” while letting countless people continue to suffer.

This lackadaisical attitude shows that health and safety are not the primary concern of those in power. Surely a simple statement to Indonesia to prevent this situation from happening again could be the domino effect for lasting change. To do nothing means allowing this to continue and people to suffer. They have not done nearly enough within their role as the people’s representatives to protect people’s interests.

Suggestions have been made, for example by the Malaysian Human Rights Commission, to use the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) as a mechanism to put pressure on member states. Even if that suggestion is not taken up, something else could be done. A statement, denouncement, or the cutting of ties would put pressure on the perpetrators and protect citizens.

Deliberate state inaction is lazy and assumes people will just accept what is being said. But if those who hold the power to change policies and influence relations with other nations won’t take action, then the people must come together, demand change and hold the politicians and the companies accountable for their actions.

author: José Soeiro, Maria Manuel Rola
title: A new cycle of struggle in Portugal
content:
At the end of last June, the left and the labour movement in Portugal secured an unlikely victory: the government’s proposed labour reform, which would have overhauled the Labour Code from top to bottom, was defeated in parliament.

Public pressure was so intense — with two general strikes, dozens of protests and a campaign that rallied the majority of public opinion against the government’s violently regressive agenda — that the far right, fearful of the electoral consequences of seeing its support for such a thoroughly unpopular proposal through to the end, changed its position and ultimately joined forces with the left to vote down the government’s labour reform package.

This struggle ushered in a new cycle of confidence for the popular movement.

The government, which holds a minority in parliament, put labour issues on hold and sought to change the subject. It ensured that the Socialist Party [PS] abstained on the draft state budget, on the one hand, and, on the other, reached an agreement with the far right on a new rental law which, in practice, virtually eliminates any rights for tenants.

A two-month delay in paying rent can lead to eviction. There is no longer a cap on deposits for renting a property. The number of months’ rent a tenant must pay in advance when signing a tenancy agreement has been increased to three. The 2% cap on rent increases has been removed.

With this proposal, the rental market — which is used by those unable to buy a home — becomes even more cut-throat, in the euro zone country where house prices have risen the most, where only 2% of housing is social housing, where the rent per square metre has doubled over the last five years, where, on average, people spend 50 per cent of their income on rent for legally registered tenancies alone (that is to say, it is even worse if we take the informal market into account), and where the poverty rate rises from around 15% to 27% when housing costs are factored in.

The rising cost of living, including fuel prices, and the approval (albeit without a final vote yet) of the tenancy law have created the conditions for a new cycle of protests.

A coalition of various groups and associations, called “Não Dá Mais” (“We Can’t Take It Anymore”), organised demonstrations against the rising cost of living in five cities, on October 10, attended by several thousand people. In Porto, which has the greatest impact in the north of the country, this demonstration coincided with two other protests — in support of Palestine and to safeguard an old market (the Bulhão), which is highly symbolic for the city — and was followed by a call, inspired by events in Spain and the wave of outrage over Maricarmen’s death, to set up a tent camp at the end of the rally, occupying the square where it had taken place.

On the first night, around 30 tents were pitched and remained in place. On the second night, there were more than 50. The camp was going to be cleared by the council at the end of the second night. The activists used social media to call for a new demonstration at the same location, with the aim of deciding, at an open-air public assembly, whether to resume the sit-in. On that same day, the Mayor declared that he would be “absolutely uncompromising” if the square were to be occupied with tents again. But not even that deterred the organisers of the camp, who set it up once more, with more people and more support.

At 3am, with no journalists left in the square, the government and the city council, acting in concert, ordered a brutal police charge against a few dozen peaceful activists who had spent the night in that square. Curiously, this was on the very same day that, 20 years ago, a movement had begun to occupy the municipal theatre located in the same square.

The mobile phone videos shocked public opinion and the city. That very same day, thousands of people flocked to the square in outrage, in a massive demonstration that also made its way to the entrance of the city hall. Not only did the movement explode, but it also began to spark reactions in other cities and a huge wave of solidarity.

Not even the attempts by the government and some commentators to stigmatise and blame the activists for having “provoked the police” had any effect.

For the past 10 days, the square has been constantly filled with thousands of people in the late afternoon and evening, with cultural events and workshops, whilst the organisers manage the day-to-day running of catering, security and cleaning. A new camp also sprang up in Lisbon last weekend, and in Coimbra.

At the trade union demonstration called by the CGTP (Portugal’s largest trade union confederation) against the rising cost of living on the 17th, trade union organisations and the “campers” converged, forming a crowd of diverse ages and social backgrounds, which returned to the square in Porto. That same evening, the Porto camp was re-established with thousands of people, and several hundred spending the night there.

A new cycle of protests has begun and will reach its next major national milestone on November 14 with a national demonstration.

At present, it is impossible to predict how the movement will develop. The issue of housing, however, is already at the centre of public debate, even as the government attempts to refocus the debate on “violence” or the legitimacy of occupying a public space with tents.

Progress has been made, notably during the demonstrations on October 17, in developing a convergence between the housing protests and the trade union mobilisations. The political parties are under pressure to provide answers regarding the housing crisis, and the far right is already beginning to backtrack on its commitments regarding the new tenancy law, which may thus be defeated by popular mobilisation, as happened with the government’s labour reform package.

There is also discussion as to what effect the Spanish general strike will have on the timetable and repertoire of struggles in Portugal. Undoubtedly, the inertia has been shaken off and we are facing a new cycle of collective action, with significant youth participation, which is already fostering a new collective consciousness and may have lasting effects on the reorganisation of the popular movement and the balance of power in the country.

[Reprinted from International Viewpoint.]

author: Ben Radford
title: UN General Assembly votes to end US blockade of Cuba — again
content:
The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has overwhelmingly voted to end the United States government’s cruel and illegal economic blockade of Cuba. One-hundred-and-thirty countries voted in favour of the resolution on the “Necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba” on October 28, with 17 against and 25 abstentions.

Every year since 1992, the UNGA has overwhelmingly voted to end the blockade. However, this year, there was a rise in votes against and abstentions, likely reflective of new far-right governments — for example, in Colombia, Chile and Honduras — coming to power since last year’s vote. The US has also ramped up its international efforts to isolate Cuba through sanctions and threats of sanctions against countries that trade with Cuba.

This year’s vote took place as escalating US economic warfare against Cuba is causing a devastating humanitarian crisis. The blockade’s impacts have been characterised as a “silent genocide”, severely restricting Cubans’ access to food, medicine, equipment and fuel, and impacting every aspect of daily life.

The Cuban government submitted its annual report to the UNGA in September, detailing last year’s impacts of the US blockade. Between March last year and February this year, the blockade inflicted more than US$8 billion worth of damages.

The economic cost of just four days of the blockade amounts to the cost of all fuel imports needed to meet Cuba’s demand.

On top of existing strangulation mechanisms, the US government imposed an energy blockade on Cuba in January, claiming that the country posed an “unusual and extraordinary threat” to US national security.

The US announced tariffs on goods from countries that, directly or indirectly, sold or provided oil to Cuba. Following the US’s January 3 attacks on Venezuela, it also blocked all Venezuelan oil shipments to the country.

The energy blockade is the reason for widespread blackouts, as well as disruptions to water supply, waste collection and transport.

The fuel shortages are severely impacting hospital operations, including treatments that require a steady energy supply, such as haemodialysis. There are harrowing reports of surgeons having to perform operations by mobile phone lights, due to the blackouts.

The US blockade has affected Cubans’ access to vital treatment and medicine. One example is Cuba’s cancer survival rates, which, while still higher than many low- and middle-income countries, have dropped from 85% to 65%.

Cuba’s infant mortality has risen from 4 out of 1000 live births in 2018 to 9.9 last year — a 148% rise.

Cuban authorities say that the current transport crisis is more acute than during the “Special Period” in the 1990s following the collapse of the Soviet Union, which plunged Cuba into a prolonged economic crisis. Fuel shortages have affected refrigerated transport, preventing more than 30,000 children from receiving vaccines.

In May, the US imposed a regime of secondary sanctions against governments and companies that invest in or trade with Cuba.

For example, the US Office of Foreign Assets Control has imposed fines on US companies for handling cargo shipments bound for Cuba and providing services for people living in the country.

Over the past year, 34 international banking institutions suspended or declined to conduct operations with Cuba, citing risks of secondary sanctions.

Several airlines have ceased operations in Cuba and many international hotel chains also abandoned management agreements for hotels, citing the risks posed by the secondary sanctions regime. These sanctions — along with other US measures — have contributed to the collapse in Cuba’s tourism industry.

“The application of these measures has produced a sophisticated mechanism of asphyxiation directed at the Cuban population, exceeding by far the levels of pressure historically imposed over decades,” the annual report said.

It also notes that the blockade has caused US$3.9 trillion worth of damages since it was imposed. However, it said the impacts go far beyond economic losses, causing suffering, illness and death.

The US blockade of Cuba violates not just international law, but any semblance of humanity.

The US government has made its intention of achieving “regime change” in Cuba by the end of the year very clear; it is openly considering the possibility of military attacks. This has been the US’s policy since Cubans overthrew the US-backed Fulgencio Batista military dictatorship in 1959 and set about implementing a planned economy based on meeting people’s needs.

Since then, the US has undertaken or sponsored terrorist attacks, a military invasion and an economic blockade against the Cuban people, with the explicit aim of bringing about “hunger, desperation and overthrow of government”, as revealed by a 1960 US memorandum.

Ahead of the UNGA vote, the Cuban Embassy in Australia told Green Left that despite the challenges facing Cuba, it “remains committed to its social development and international cooperation”.

It noted that the Australian government voted in favour of last year’s UNGA resolution, calling for an end to the US blockade on Cuba.

The embassy encouraged the Labor government to engage in “constructive dialogue and to explore practical avenues of cooperation with Cuba in areas such as health, education, disaster resilience, renewable energy and scientific research”.

“At a time when the world faces complex economic, environmental and humanitarian challenges, greater engagement and cooperation with Cuba, rather than continued sanctions, would benefit both the Cuban people and the international community.”

Since 1963, Cuba has sent more than 600,000 health professionals overseas to provide care and train personnel, mostly in low-income regions. The US aims to destroy Cuba’s model of medical internationalism, pressuring countries to terminate often decades-long Cuban medical missions.

More than 160 countries have benefited from Cuba’s medical internationalism, including its pandemic and disaster response to free training for tens of thousands of medical personnel.

The embassy also said that it “deeply appreciates” the Australian solidarity movement with Cuba, saying it has “demonstrated a steadfast commitment to friendship and cooperation between our peoples” over many years.

“Through educational activities, public advocacy, cultural exchanges and community engagement, solidarity organisations and supporters across Australia have played a valuable role in raising awareness about the impact of the blockade and in promoting closer people-to-people ties.

“The annual vote at the United Nations is an important reminder of the overwhelming international rejection of the blockade and the need for policies that promote development, mutual respect and people-to-people exchange.”

author: Binoy Kampark
title: Unmasked agendas: Macron, youth protests and blocking social media
content:
Finally, the ill-fitting mask on the ugly face of government policy comes off. In the sunset of his administration, French President Emmanuel Macron is facing a boiling, indignant movement that began with the protests of disgruntled students and has burgeoned into something much more significant.

Teachers at the Antoine de Saint-Exupéry High School in the southeastern Parisian suburb of Créteil went on strike over severe staff shortages, on September 17. Students and parents added themselves to the strike. The school entrance was blocked, videos taken and social media platforms used to disseminate the message.

A blooming followed through to October, drawing in some 3700 schools and hundreds and thousands of protesters. Social, economic and political angst had been stirred, with grievances focused on inadequate provision of teaching, packed classrooms, overburdened schedules and the dilapidation of school infrastructure. The university admissions platform Parcoursup also came in for criticism.

As part of the response to the protests, Macron has, as is traditional with a smug incumbent caught off guard, identified an aggravating, foreign influence steering matters. Conveniently for him, the fault seems to lie with the progenitors of the social media world, those United States Big Tech beasts and platforms that have turned users into anything from bovine consumers to adept, resourceful users of technology. It’s the resourceful aspect of the technology that is proving particularly troubling for government officialdom.

As one of the last acts of his administration, France’s desperate leader has attempted to impose age-restrictions on users of social media platforms ostensibly as a therapeutic exercise.

In doing so, he has joined a wide tent of invigilating governments keen to use the alleged malignancies of social media as an alibi for controlling access to certain online platforms, a mood captured by the efforts of the European Union to advance the all suppressing EU Kids Act. (Australia was the first to bolt out of the stables last December with its Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024, paraded as a noble effort to limit the use of social platforms by those under 16 years of age. Unsurprisingly, it is showing itself to be a foolish legislative bauble, weak and circumvented.)

On July 21, the French parliament adopted the “Loi visant à protéger les mineurs face aux risques associés à l’usage des réseaux sociaux” (Law aiming to protect minors from the risks associated with social media usage), an alleged palliative for the ills (examples include anxiety, depression and sleep disorders) of using social media for those under 15. This exaggerated sense of moral success did not last long.

In August, France’s Constitutional Council poured cold water on the government’s grand strategy, striking down the legislation as needlessly broad and hopelessly excessive. The access to the platforms, for instance, was “not subject to any condition relating to the functionalities or content offered, the dangers they expose users, and the inadequacy of the safeguards with which they are provided.”

Saliently, the Council noted that the ban encumbered the rights of young people to access information and engage in the democratic system. This meant retarding the useful instruction of children to meaningfully engage the political process on ceasing to be minors. Social networking platforms were not inherently wicked things; they could also serve as educational tools, promote civic engagement and aid in building communities.

A chastened Macron proceeded to direct Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu to make the necessary adjustments in line with the Council’s decision.

The response from Macron to these youth-inspired protests, in light of his stuttering efforts against the corruptions of social media, is a more candid reflection on why governments seek to restrict any platform that adds vim to dissent and disagreement.

In remarks made to members of law enforcement during his October 26 visit to Marseille City Hall, the president scorned social media sites for “damaging our democracies” and being “tools for mobilising the worst impulses”. They had brought “young and not-so-young people to places where criminal acts, attacks and looting were taking place.”

This imprecise, misleading assessment proved most telling.

In the week leading up to October 24, recent reports reveal that the French interior ministry was putting feelers out to telecom operators regarding restricting access to social networks. Discussions also considered the possibility of restricting mobile internet altogether in specific areas.

In simple terms, the Macron administration was considering the very sort of thing it freely accuses non-Western authoritarian governments of doing.

According to an unnamed employee from a telecommunications provider, speaking to Politico, “What they wanted, above all, was to block the communication channels that allow gangs to meet up and organise.”

The digital outlet Blast shed much blessed light on the proposed response in obtaining a letter allegedly sent by Lecornu on October 22 to the directors of the four chief telecom companies: Christel Heydemann of Orange, Benoît Torloting of Bouygues Telecom, Thomas Reynaud of the iliad Group, and Arthur Dreyfus of Altice France.

The PM sought power to “temporarily suspend access” provided by the companies to Snapchat, TikTok, and Instagram in the event urban violence was to recur. (The X platform was subsequently added to the list.) The directors were to ready themselves for such a temporary suspension to take place over the weekend of October 24–25 to avert what had taken place between October 17 and 18, namely, the coordination of organised looting, communication about potential targets, the movement of groups, and the locations of law enforcement.

The minutes of the meeting between high-ranking government officials from the General Secretariat of the government, the PM’s office, the Directorate General for Enterprise and legal experts from the four operators show a lack of consensus.

Government suggestions to limit mobile phones to certain areas were rebuffed: the operators did not have the means of imposing limited, temporary blocks. In any case, alternative messaging services, such as a VPN, would suffice to circumvent such measures.

The proposed measures were ultimately, and enlighteningly stymied. The fact that they were considered at all shows, yet again, that regulating the internet and its various platforms has little to do with Edenic children or their welfare but much to do about limiting the inconveniences of free speech and the means of protesting against a rotten status quo.

[Binoy Kampmark lectures at RMIT University.]

author: Mat Ward
title: 10 new underrated protest albums that should be topping the charts
content:
Do you think there’s no good protest music these days? So did I, until I started looking for it. Every month, I listen to it all, then select the best that relates to that month’s political news. Here’s the round-up for October.

New South Wales' Labor government backed Queensland's ban on Palestine freedom slogans on October 1. The move came as Jewish US protest singer David Rovics released probably his catchiest album yet, containing songs "all about the US-Israeli Epstein Empire", before touring Australia. On album opener "The Holocaust Is Now", featuring backing vocals from Green Left writer Kamala Emanuel, he sings: "Can you spend two hundred dollars to buy a loaf of bread? Neither can the Palestinians, they’re dying instead." The LP was released while donkey prices in Gaza surged from $US1000 to $US30,000 "due to the virtual elimination of motorised private transport". As Israel's election loomed on October 28, the album's title track, "Rise", called for Israelis to rise up against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who was being endorsed by US President Donald Trump as a "great warrior" who must be re-elected so they could "finish the job" in their disastrous war on Iran. "Overthrow your theocratic state, before it is too late," sings Rovics. "Reject your leaders and their lies. Rise, Israelis, rise!" LISTEN>>>

One of the seemingly few Israelis rising up is pop-rock musician Regev Baruch, with his scathing new album, Super Sparta. Its title is a phrase coined by Netanyahu last year to describe his commitment to eternal war. Discussing the LP, which likens Israelis to Nazis, Baruch said: “There’s this graffiti that says, ‘Grandma, what were you doing during the genocide?’ I was looking for a good answer to that — something I could do to prove I wasn’t part of the silent majority... In the end, I said, ‘OK, there are journalists; they’re investigating. There are lawyers; they’re fighting a legal battle. You’re a musician — just make music.’ That’s the most powerful thing I can do.” Of course, Baruch is far from the only Jewish person publicly condemning Israel's genocide against Palestinians, as shown by the countless Jews who attended vigils marking three years of the war on October 7. Meanwhile, pro-Palestine punks Amyl and the Sniffers, whose new live LP blasts fascistic leaders, said they were donating proceeds from an upcoming Bondi gig to "extend our love" to Jews affected by the Bondi attack. LISTEN>>>

English feminist rage musician Delilah Bon, who paints her body with slogans such as "Free Palestine", also released a new live album on October 16 as her Australian tour loomed. The LP documents a show she played to reach out to American fans after she had to cancel a US tour due to fears about the country's Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. The event, which raised £8,000 for organisations supporting people affected by ICE, opens with the apt "Illegal Aliens" and powers through fan favourites such as "Dead Men Don't Rape", "War On Women" and "Princeless Princess". On the excoriating "Not The President", she sings: "That's not the president, that's just some man, who has abused so many women and children... There's so much love in this world, I'm holding hands with every girl that cries alone in her room, that fears this world is so fucking doomed." She then gets her British fans to chant "fuck Trump" for their peers in the US. The explosive power of her dayglo-daubed live show, in which she goes from pitch-perfect singing to razor-sharp rapping and searing screaming, is inspiring. LISTEN>>>

Also condemning ICE is the new LP from Grammy-winning folk musician Mary Gauthier, released days before an agent in New York shot into a car with a child inside. On "Soldier Of Fortune" she cites ICE victims Renée Good and Alex Pretti as she sings: "You're nothing but a gun for hire, hiding behind a mask. You didn't care if she was somebody's mother, when you shot her in the face through the window glass. A VA nurse on a city street, full of the courage you lack. An angel of mercy, helping a stranger and you fired 10 bullets into his back." That preceded the October 16 LP from Heavens To Betsy, the kind of riot grrrl pioneers who paved the way for the likes of Delilah Bon. The LP, a long-lost 1992 demo released to mark their reformation, centres on "My Secret" in which singer Corin Tucker blasts an abuser. "It turned the tables on everything, and it let go of everything, and it also freaked everyone out," she recalled. "It was incredible. It changed my life in a way." Following in their footsteps are riot grrrl punks Piss, who released their new, critically-acclaimed album on October 30. LISTEN>>>

One of the few men to speak up for abused women is Irish electronic punk Meryl Streek, on his new album, released on October 9. On "Kelly", the spoken-word artist details what he calls "an ongoing criminal investigation, currently classified as a 'Contested Cause of Death'". "It wasn't even considered a crime scene at the time," he seethes in the song. "93 different bruises laying upon this girl's body." Streek says the LP, titled Stories They Don't Teach You At School, "serves as an alternative form of education... with core values of compassion, resilience, and community — themes rarely explored within a classroom setting". As if to illustrate his point, a fortnight later, it was reported that the owner of Mount Pleasant coal mine near Muswellbrook in Australia was trying to influence the school curriculum to make it pro-fossil fuels. The news came after the mine's expansion was blocked by the High Court on climate grounds, but then allowed by New South Wales Premier Chris Minns. He approved it just five days after holding a fundraiser attended by industry lobby group Coal Australia. LISTEN>>>

The effect of such moves really hits home on the new album by US indie rockers Diiv. Their previous album, 2024's Frog in Boiling Water, compared the way humans are dealing with climate change to the way frogs refuse to jump out of a slowly heating pan before boiling to death. Their new LP, released on October 30, comes after singer Zachary Cole Smith's home was destroyed in the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires. Its song "Evangelizer" depicts a “post-capitalist hellscape” and "The Crash" contains a call to “throw the billionaires screaming in an alligator pit”. Likewise, the new album by Death Valley Girls was influenced by lead singer Bonnie Bloomgarden’s home being destroyed by the same wildfires. On album closer "How Losing Everything in the Fire Taught Me to Love Myself" she sings: "Soon the fear will turn to pain and the pain is a sign you’ll get through this again... even when I have nothing I have all I need, soon I’ll come back a stronger version of me". The band say the album's title is "a welcome from the natural world to a species that has largely forgotten its place within it". LISTEN>>>

Also lamenting the loss of the natural world as a monster El Nino looms is country-pop mega star Sheryl Crow on her new album, released on October 9. On its song "Flat Earth", the "All I Wanna Do" hitmaker sings: "The Amazon River has finally all but dried up. Mother Nature's been patient, but now she's had enough. There's gotta be a better way, I don't wanna hide away." And on "Freedom Bus", a collaboration with viral protest singer Jesse Welles, she sings: "What if everyone took a civics class? I'm not sure I know anyone who'd pass. But how wе live today comes from the past. If wе forget, it could slip from our grasp... Whoever said freedom was free? There ain't no freedom without history, and folks who died for you and me, so don't be an asshole, let everyone be." The album comes after she released a song slamming Trump, who she often publicly criticises. “Is it science fiction or prediction wrapped in George Orwell?” she sang on last year's "The New Normal". “If the news is fake and fear is hate and nothing’s immoral, to the leader of the free world, then welcome to the new normal.” LISTEN>>>

Trump's friend and funder, transphobic trillionaire Elon Musk, became the world's richest person by exploiting technology. Ironic, then, that the "father of theoretical computer science", Alan Turing, was persecuted for being gay in the 1950s. That point is the centrepiece of the new concept album by queer electronic hitmakers the Pet Shop Boys. The LP, released on October 9, tells Turing's extraordinary life story. “We became fascinated with the story because it has a tragedy, because he was gay and it was illegal to be gay during those days,” singer Neil Tennant explained. This meant that, despite Turing helping to break the enigma code during World War Two, he was arrested for gross indecency in 1952 and died two years later. “We followed his story from a personal level and the scientific and codebreaking level,” said Tennant. Three days after the album's release, queer media outlet LGBTQ Nation reported that in Alex Gibney's new four-hour documentary about Musk, "Musk’s ex-wife says he cut off his trans daughter’s health insurance the day after she came out". LISTEN>>>

Musk is also skewered on the innovative new album by feminist Bristol rapper B of Briz, released on October 6. On "Who left the Overton Window open?", the emcee, who holds a PhD in philosophy, raps about the term depicting the range of acceptable political thought. "Oh no, you guys, I'm afraid you might have left the Overton Window open," she mocks, "when one of the world’s richest men seig heiled on the world stage, Doge’d all over every page, decimated international aid, and you let him still be a Fellow of the Royal Society." And on "Dear Antifa", she addresses the anti-fascist movement as she spits: "Dear Antifa, it’s me, again, B, writing another letter and you’re the addressee, but I’m beginning to think you’re not there, you’re not anywhere. Friends, I reckon Antifa might just be you and me! An idea in the hearts of decent people, and apparently absent in the venal. Present in the people who don’t want to persecute minorities or defend misogyny. People who see concentration camps and detention centres as a moral repugnancy." LISTEN>>>

At least plenty of artists see detention centres as a moral repugnancy, as shown by a 47-track fundraiser against ICE released on October 2. Artist and activist Dali Colorado said she was inspired to compile the LP after Ambrocio "Enrique" Lozano, a well-known ice cream street vendor in LA, was detained by ICE. A photo of his abandoned cart soon went viral, inspiring the album's artwork. The LP includes famous names among many more underground musicians. author: Jim McIlroy
title: New film showcases people’s blockade of world’s biggest coal port
content:
About 150 people filled the Ashfield Town Hall auditorium on October 10 for the Gadigal/Sydney premiere of environmental group Rising Tide’s new short film, Taking the Channel.

The film showcases the People’s Blockade of the world’s biggest coal port, which took place in Muloobinba/Newcastle, in November last year.

Taking the Channel features interviews with activists who took part in the blockade, as well as dramatic footage of the hundreds of people on their kayaks setting out from Horseshoe Beach to confront a giant coal ship attempting to pass through the Newcastle Port’s entrance.

During the film, it is revealed that several coal ships were directly turned around by the blockade, while up to a dozen others were cancelled by the authorities as a result of the mass action by activists.

Interviews with participants include a grandmother from Adelaide contemplating challenging the law by going out on the water: “Am I able to go through with it?” she says. But then she shows her determination to go ahead, when she feels the strength of the large number of people taking action on the day.

A young coal worker says that he and many of his co-workers are forced to work in the fossil fuel industry not because they want to, but because they have no readily available alternative jobs at present. “It is time for action,” he says, not only to stop the coal ships, but for government

author: Sam Wainwright
title: Reject the AUKUS death machine, join the fight for the future
content:
The nuclear powered submarine USS Colorado docked at the HMAS Stirling naval base on Menadup/Garden Island, five kilometres from Rockingham in Perth’s southern suburbs, on October 27.

The vessel is in port for a month of maintenance exercises in preparation for the Submarine Rotational Force — West program which will start in September next year, being the first of four United States’ and one British nuclear powered submarines based at HMAS Stirling.

Its arrival was an opportunity for Labor to insist that AUKUS is “on track”, without resolving any of the significant cost and time blow-outs associated with the plan to build the SSN-AUKUS class submarines.

It also means that HMAS Stirling has become a de facto US navy base, with its submarines and crew not just visiting, but stationed in Western Australia, allowing the US to qualitatively step up its presence in the Indian Ocean.

When AUKUS was announced five years ago, in the shadow of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, we were told it was necessary in order to uphold a mythical “rules based order”. Since then, Israel has gone on a genocidal rampage with the support of western governments.

Any hope that US President Donald Trump’s violent rejection of international law, in both word and deed, might lead the Anthony Albanese government to have second thoughts about integrating Australia ever more tightly with US military strategy, through AUKUS and the Force Posture Agreement, has been smashed on the rocks.

The opposite is true. Neither Albanese, foreign minister Penny Wong or defence minister Richard Marles have spoken against Trump’s rampage across the world; be it the kidnapping of the Venezuelan president, threats against Greenland and Canada, the criminal blockade of Cuba, bombing of Iran or the the cruelly misnamed "Board of Peace” foisted on Gaza.

When Wong was directly asked by a journalist whether she agreed that the war on Iran was a breach of the United Nations Charter, the best she could manage was this mealy-mouthed response — “It’s up to the US and Israel to explain the legality of their actions”.

While the Albanese government might still cloak its domestic neoliberal economic agenda in some token progressive rhetoric and gestures to mark out some space between it and the Coalition, its foreign policy is now completely subordinate to Trump’s.

Reinforcing this orientation is the long established ambition of both Labor and Liberal to make Australia one of the world's top ten weapons exporters, further tightening integration with both US and Israeli weapons manufacturers.

Trump’s decision to boost US military spending by 50% on 2025 levels by 2027 has turned this push into a stampede as Australian governments, businesses and universities fall over themselves to try to get a slice of the action.

Meanwhile, urgent action to address the real existential threat to humanity posed by runaway global warming is stalled, demonstrated by the approval of new and expanded fossil fuel projects and Labor’s lowering of expectations ahead of the COP31 climate summit.

Capitalism, based on the endless search for profits and growth, is incapable of solving the climate crisis.

Since the industrial revolution, every new source of energy — biomass, coal, oil, nuclear and renewables — has added to energy production, not replaced it. In other words capitalism welcomes renewables, but in addition to fossil fuels, not instead of them.

Both the federal government and senior military strategists are perfectly well aware of this, just as they know that this will lead to climate breakdown, social crisis and war.

Consequently the real long term climate plan of the Albanese government is increased repression at home and war abroad. It’s not an exaggeration to say that militarism is their deadly serious response to the climate crisis.

Confronting and dismantling AUKUS, the Force Posture Agreement and the weapons industry is central to the fight for a safe climate.

A certain amount of catastrophic warming is already baked into the system. Even if we do everything materially possible to halt and reverse warming starting today, we still face massive ecological disruption. But this is no excuse for giving up.

Replacing a society based on greed, that is pushing us to ecological collapse and war, with a society based on human solidarity is necessary to face the climate crisis. But we face serious obstacles in the fight to pull humanity back from the brink.

Modern day capitalists represent the most powerful and violent ruling class in human history, when measured by the sheer number of innocent lives they are prepared to sacrifice to defend their system.

Furthermore, in a relatively wealthy country like Australia, a section of the population is prepared to give their loyalty to the empire in return for a few extra crumbs off the capitalist table, despite the cost to our sisters and brothers in the Global South.

This includes that section of business, workers, and indeed sections of the union movement, who put aside considerations of their children’s future in exchange for profits or well paid jobs in the “defence” industry death machine.

Many more well paid jobs could be generated by directing war spending to social services — public transport, health, education, public housing and environmental repair — but you have to believe that is possible in order to be convinced.

This won’t happen simply through abstract alternative visions or by convincing people that Trump’s vision of the world is profoundly sociopathic. It will grow out of each and every struggle against the war drive and fossil fuel expansion.

The youth rebellion ripping across the world is a symbol of hope. Change is both possible and necessary.

There’s no time to waste, join us in the fight for the future.

[Sam Wainwright is a national co-convenor of the Socialist Alliance.]

author: Diane de Vignemont
title: ‘If we burn, you burn with us’: France’s youth ignite a massive revolt
content:
While media fixated on the violence in Paris, French high school students achieved something rare and important on October 17–18: sectors that usually fight alone marched together in massive protests that are seeing repercussions around Europe.

Truthdig's Diane de Vignemont spoke to high school students, educators and others at the protest in Paris about their demands and how the movement is evolving.

“Make sure you tell the Americans that trash cans aren’t the only things burning in France,” 16-year-old Ewen told Truthdig as protesters gathered on the Place de la République on Saturday [October 17]. Tear gas canisters had been falling into the growing crowd for about an hour, and the teen struggled to make himself heard with his mask.

“Our future is burning, too,” Ewen added. Due to the repression and arrests by police, most protesters asked that only their first names be used.

In rapid succession, he listed everything he’d come to protest against: his rat-infested high school, the violent police repression of the student movement, but also the lack of hospital beds across the country, the cost of living, the saturated job market and the quickly-forgotten fires that ravaged France this summer. During the country’s hottest summer on record this year, some 250,000 acres of forest burned.

Grabbing his three friends, Ewen then posed for a photo, holding up a sign that read: “If we burn, you burn with us!”

“It’s a Hunger Games reference,” Ewen explained, as though I were decidedly too ancient to get it on my own. “It means that we’re not just fighting for ourselves, but for you, too.”

Marine Champetier de Ribes, who teaches literature at a school in a Paris suburb, told Truthdig that she felt France’s youth had awakened something in the rest of society. “Us adults had collectively fallen into torpor,” she said. “They shook us out of it and reminded us all that we’re right to be angry.”

That torpor lifted in plain sight on October 17. Between 550,000 and 800,000 people marched across the country. Though much of the national and international coverage focused on the violence that marred the margins of Saturday’s protests, the lesson was elsewhere: In less than a month, the high schoolers’ movement managed to pull a tired, resigned country back into the streets. Students were joined by teachers, parents, doctors, nurses, lawyers, pensioners, Yellow Vests, farmers and firefighters in perhaps the most intersectional movement France has seen in decades.

Champetier de Ribes, 34, told Truthdig that she and her colleagues across the education sector had been organising for years, but had been slowly losing steam. “No one was listening to us,” she lamented.

In her school alone, she cited “cockroach-infested walls, clogged toilets, rat droppings in the microwaves and boiling classrooms that have yet to cool down after this summer’s heat waves.” Champetier de Ribes said she has also been forced to fit 38 students into her 215-square-foot classroom, which never has enough chairs and desks: “I’ve had to insist that at least three of them be absent every week so I can teach the rest,” she said.

Champetier de Ribes said teachers had become disillusioned. “We’d quite forgotten how to be angry, until, that is, our students began leading by example,” she said.

Starting on September 17, high schoolers across the country began barricading their schools to demand better material conditions and equal education opportunities. The movement began in the Paris suburb of Créteil and it spread fast: By October 1, the Interior Ministry reported that more than 1000 of France’s 3700 high schools had been affected, more than 200 of them blockaded.

The students’ demands are more specific than their critics let on: a 10 billion-euro investment plan for schools, and an end to Parcoursup, the national platform that manages university admissions, which is often compared to a “social sorting machine” and criticised for its lack of transparency.

They’re also asking for more teachers, Last year, students across France lost some 20 million hours worth of lessons because absent teachers were not replaced. The education shortfalls are a result of President Emmanuel Macron’s neoliberal approach to public education funding while simultaneously increasing defense spending.

Teachers, in turn, organised to support their pupils. “They write the rules and we follow,” Champetier de Ribes said. She and her colleagues created an Instagram account to share the students’ demands with a grown-up audience: “We have to speak their language,” she added with a laugh.

From the start, the movement was met with force. The government, which chose to label the movement not as a “school protest” but as “urban violence,” sent police riot squads directly into high schools and universities.

Eden, 14, had his jaw fractured and most of his teeth knocked after being struck in the face by a tear gas grenade in a Paris suburb, leaving him, according to his mother, barely able to eat through a straw in his hospital bed. A 15-year-old in the north had his hand torn off by a so-called anti-encirclement grenade. On Saturday, in the eastern town of Mulhouse, Maïssa, 17, was struck by a tear-gas canister and lost her left eye.

Some 6773 minors have been taken into police custody since the protests began in mid-September. Complaints are currently being filed across the country for verbal and physical mistreatment of these high schoolers during their detention.

This level of violence gave teachers yet another cause for concern, Champetier de Ribes said. “We were, to put it plainly, terrified at the very idea of seeing our students face off with the police.” Five months pregnant, she herself cannot physically protect her students, as tear gas is highly toxic. But she did help her colleagues prepare emergency kits. Identified with a white armband, these teachers carry masks, saline solution, bandages, disinfectant, water and applesauce pouches, ready to assist their pupils should they need help.

“This generation shook us awake,” Champetier de Ribes said. “Now, we have to be there for them, and alongside them.”

Christophe, who teaches mathematics in a private Paris high school, joined the protest Saturday with a sign that read: “You should not have betrayed us. We’re here to take our future back.” He told Truthdig that, while his was not an underprivileged school, his students had nonetheless joined their peers on the street, demanding equality. “My students may not be the ones getting beat up, but they’re still children,” he said.

Down the street, as tear gas dispersed the musicians of the New World Orchestra, another sign read: “Too young to be listened to, big enough to get beaten up.”

“I initially thought the movement seemed a bit harebrained,” 50-year-old Rachid told Truthdig at Saturday’s protest. The family doctor, who asked that his last name be withheld, had been perplexed by the high schoolers’ scattered demands and confused by the odd costumes and the “aura battles” they performed on the barricades in front of their schools.

“I thought this was another one of these social media trends I simply no longer understand,” he quipped.

But after his daughter’s classmates were heavily tear-gassed by the police, and still came back the next day, he began seeing things differently. “These kids, I realised, have a good head on their shoulders,” Rachid said. He joined the movement on October 6, alongside his daughter.

He is not alone in that. Champetier de Ribes has noticed a similar shift. “There’s a realisation, even among people who initially disapproved of the movement. They saw the level of violence, saw how far the government was prepared to go to repress this movement, and decided to put themselves on the line, too,” she said.

Rachid attended Saturday’s protest in his white coat, emblazoned with the words, “Firefighters and healthcare workers stand in solidarity.”

This was not Rachid’s first protest. As the COVID-19 pandemic ravaged the healthcare sector, he marched alongside thousands of colleagues — those the entire country had applauded night after night — in 2020. They asked for more beds, more ventilators, more money and better training. “But no matter how hard we tried, our movement remained confined to the healthcare sector,” he said.

For years, each grievance has produced its own constituency, its own demonstration, its own cycle of exhaustion. French hospital workers marched for funding, teachers protested cuts and education reforms, retirees took to the street to protect their pensions, farmers blocked roads to protest rising costs of production, Yellow Vests swarmed the Champs Élysées to demand lower gas prices. Time and time again, crowds gathered, the political class attempted to respond, and the country moved on.

The oft-aspired to “convergence des luttes” (convergence of struggles) never materialised. Until, that is, students disrupted that routine.

“This,” Rachid said as a young kilt-clad protester dressed the bronze statue of Marianne, personifying the French Republic, in a yellow vest, “is a different kind of beast entirely.”

The students’ insistence that their own futures are at stake has helped make connections between movements visible. In the presence of teenagers who refuse to accept that their future must be worse than their parents’ present, older demonstrators have found it harder to justify their own resignation.

“What we have here is a convergence not of struggles, but of anger,” Rachid said.

“We are very angry,” 18-year-old Juliette G told Truthdig. A first-year student in political science at Sciences Po Paris, she deplored the “small-mindedness” of her elders, who balked at the intersectionality of the students’ demands.

“This is a student movement,” she said. “It’s also a feminist one, an anti-racist one, an ecologist one.” The variety of the students’ demands does not make them weaker, but stronger, she said. “Just because we’re doing things differently does not mean we are wrong.”

Her demands for intersectionality were echoed by Julie, a 27-year-old engineer Truthdig met on Saturday. “I’m glad we’ve not left them to protest alone,” she said as a group of youth set a car on fire at the far corner of the square. But said she was concerned that their wide-ranging demands for a better future would get lost if “adults” began framing the movement in terms not of justice, but of violence.

“The youth are sick of being oldsplained,” her sign read.

Behind her, Truthdig met two Latin American immigrants who had come to march in defense of democracy. Damien, 56, from Chile, carried a sign likening Macron’s repression of the youth movement to Augusto Pinochet’s in the 1970s in his country. “We’ve lived through this before,” he said. Carmen, 58, from Brazil, carried a heart-covered sign that read: “Let our children protest.”

“We’re here for Lula, too,” Carmen told Truthdig, referring to Brazil’s left-leaning President Luiz Inácio Lula de Silva, who is currently running against a Donald Trump-backed, far-right candidate.

Damien voiced his opposition to Chile’s José Antonio Kast and Argentina’s Javier Milei. “I may not be French, but I raised my daughter here, and I know your republic’s motto: ‘Liberté, Egalité, Fraternité.’ We have to show the world that we stand with these kids,” Carmen said.

Down the street, Lucie, 15, who attends a private Paris high school, held up a sign that read: “Sorry for the inconvenience, we’re trying to save our future.”

Champetier de Ribes told Truthdig she was “gobsmacked” to see privileged youth join the movement en masse. “The macronie [Macron’s political caste] is built on division and has been getting away with taking from some because they give to others,” she said. But this “doesn’t seem to work on young people — they’re not duped by efforts to divide them. They are fully aware that it’s absolute bullshit.”

“I’m incredibly proud of my students,” she said.

author: Cas Smith
title: Brazil: Lula’s election victory was won in the streets
content:
Australia’s Brazilian community joined their compatriots worldwide in a wave of street mobilisations in support of incumbent President Luiz Inácio “Lula” da Silva, ahead of his election victory on October 25.

Lula, who was first elected president in 2002, pulled ahead of right-wing opponent Flávio Bolsonaro — the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro — winning the second round run-off election by 4.4 million votes.

Significantly, this came after Bolsonaro won the first round on October 4, which prompted Brazilians to hit the streets in a significant movement to bolster Lula’s profile, and to prevent a “second Bolsonaro” presidency.

Students and the country’s working class largely led these mobilisations, which included a gathering of more than one million Lula supporters on Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana Beach the day before the election.

Around Australia, similar protests were held prior to the election, including at Scarborough Beach in Boorloo/Perth, on October 22. Organiser Pedro told Green Left that many Brazilians were afraid their country could become mired in corruption and instability under a Bolsonaro government.

“Unfortunately, we experienced Bolsonaro snr’s government for four years between 2018 and 2022,” he said.

“They were the ones in power during the [COVID-19] pandemic, which was devastating for the country in many ways, because we were denied access to vaccines and the government failed to invest in our healthcare system; the doctors were completely ignored.

“This was only a tiny part of what this government did — we have seen enough.”

Pedro said Flávio Bolsonaro’s close ties to United States President Donald Trump was a concern, highlighting Trump’s coup against Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro earlier this year and his influence on far-right Argentine President Javier Milei.

The October 25 election delivered a comprehensive win to Lula, who received 64.3 million votes, compared to Bolsonaro’s 59.8 million. This was the first time that a candidate won the presidential election after a first-round defeat.

Despite Lula’s victory, when the new Congress convenes in February next year, Bolsonaro’s party will control 28 seats in the Senate (35% of the total) and 121 seats in the lower house (24%) as well as five governorships (19%), which — once alliances are factored in — will mean the right will have bigger majorities in both houses for Lula’s next administration.

“We are trying to unite the maximum number of people in this movement,” Pedro said.

“We want to show that we are here for our freedom, our democracy, and we have something to defend against the people who are trying to take over the government again in Brazil.”

Despite Bolsonaro’s initial pledge to annul the outcome, the leader of his Liberal Party, Valdemar Costa Neto, issued a statement on October 26 accepting the election result.

Bolsonaro’s protest revolved around a last-minute extension to voting hours, which prompted him to say, in a post-election speech to supporters, that “We will take legal action.”

This was despite the fact that both sides had called for the extension: Bolsonaro’s camp said that heavy rains in the country’s south (where he enjoys popular support) would prevent people from reaching polling stations.

Lula’s side meanwhile, said that extended voting hours were necessary, citing the alleged restriction of public transport by some city administrations, which they said was an attempt to curtail the working-class vote. Bolstering this interpretation were media reports that Pablo Souza, a transportation official in the city of Salvador, had been arrested on election day.

The decision to extend voting hours was made by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin, who had been appointed to the court by Lula in 2023, and had previously been the president’s personal lawyer. These factors prompted Bolsonaro to cry foul, claiming the decision negatively impacted his voting base.

However, close analysis of the election results suggests the extension allowed for only 35,000 additional votes across Brazil, comprising 0.03% of the total. Given Lula’s victory by 4.4 million votes, this appears negligible.

Some of Bolsonaro’s supporters questioned the result, with Trump describing it as “another rigged election”. However, he did not go so far as to promise intervention on behalf of Bolsonaro.

Given Jair Bolsonaro’s failed coup against Lula after the latter’s election victory in 2022, many analysts are watching to see what his son will do next. Brazilian news outlet Folha de S.Paulo reported on October 26 that legal advisors and political allies encouraged Bolsonaro to drop his annulment request, based on Lula’s significant victory margin, in addition to its validation by the Supreme Court and election authorities.

Analysing the election, Revista Movimiento, the publication of Brazil’s Socialist Left Movement (MES), said: “The victory, however, has not resolved the country’s political contradictions. Although Lula gathered enough votes to win, the new Congress continues to be predominantly conservative, and will likely hinder any social, economic, and environmental measures or partial implementation of Lula’s program.

“Lula’s re-election demonstrates that the advantage gained in the first round was not irreversible. The combination of in-person mobilisation, digital organisation, a change in strategy and greater voter turnout allowed the president to overcome the initial disadvantage and win another term.

“The result also highlights the limitations of a presidential contest isolated from the composition of the legislature. The left won the national election, but will have to face a strengthened parliamentary opposition and a society that remains politically divided.

“The next term will therefore be marked by a dual requirement: to transform the commitments made during the campaign into concrete policies, and to preserve the mobilisation capacity that helped produce the electoral turnaround. The strength demonstrated in the streets and on social media will be an important political asset, but its influence will depend on the continuity of popular organisation and the ability to convert social support into effective achievements.”

As reported in International Viewpoint, journalist and ecosocialist Iain Bruce, who was in Brazil for the election, said: “This is the most important defeat for the far right we have seen anywhere in the world in recent times, and its impact will be felt worldwide. Seeing those millions and millions of people pour onto the streets across this vast country to celebrate was enough to make you weep.

“The seemingly impossible turnaround in the second round is not a simple electoral victory. It was won in the streets and on socials.

“Immediately after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, won in the first round, thousands of mainly very young people took to streets in Niteroi, across the bay from Rio de Janeiro, to demonstrate against the likelihood of a neo-fascist government in Brazil. The same thing happened in cities in the Northeast, the most impoverished region. This was repeated throughout the country in the three weeks between the rounds.

“In parallel, younger members of congress from a smaller party supporting Lula’s Workers Party, completely revamped the campaign’s lacklustre social media presence. Lula’s Army, a Whatsapp channel launched by André Janones of the Rede party, went from 50,000 followers to a million in two days. Now, it has 10 million.

“What the Brazilian people have achieved can be a huge inspiration for all of us facing resurgent varieties of neo-fascism and the far right in different parts of the world. But they will also need support. We should be thinking now about how to organise that solidarity.”

author: Jeff Rickertt
title: Phil Monsour’s ‘Time of Monsters’ is a call to action against Israel’s genocide
content:
Time of Monsters Phil Monsour October 2026 Pre-order the album and lyric book at: pozible.com/profile/phil-monsour. Listen now on Bandcamp.

In the mythical Anglo-Saxon poem Beowulf, an entire population is subjugated by a bloodthirsty and seemingly invincible monster, Grendel. He “ruled in defiance of right, one against all”. “Malignant by nature, he never showed remorse.” (Seamus Heaney, Beowulf: A New Verse Translation, New York, WW Norton & Co, 2000, p11.)

With the genocide in Gaza now into its fourth year, and with Israel extending its military savagery to Lebanon, Syria and Iran, and tightening its bloody grip on the West Bank and East Jerusalem, it is clear the peoples of the Middle East are also living under the sway of a monster, malignant by nature, never showing remorse.

Unable to resolve the crisis of legitimacy generated by its founding act of land theft and dispossession, unable to quell the desire of the land’s indigenous people for liberation, the Israeli state, like Grendel, lashes out in rage, resorting to ever-increasing violence to sustain its power.

Halfway across the planet, in Magan-djin/Brisbane, Australia, a new album by Phil Monsour foregrounds the trauma, resilience, courage, fears and hopes of those resisting this evil; first and foremost the Palestinians themselves, but also the millions who have mobilised globally in solidarity with them over the past three years.

This album, Time of Monsters, adds to Monsour’s already impressive body of music about colonisation and war in the Middle East. It comprises 12 songs written over the past three years, each a response to Israel’s latest genocidal escalation of its never-ending war of subjugation.

One track is a rousing cover of Macklemore’s “Hind’s Hall 2”, the only song on the album not by Monsour. Another track, “Song for Fatima Hassouna”, honours the Palestinian photojournalist murdered by the Israel Defense Forces, alongside six members of her family, in April last year. The other songs respond to the genocide and Western complicity thematically. They invoke the visceral monstrousness of it, framing their narratives around recurring motifs: barbarism, loss, grief, survival, love and hope. The style is acoustic rock, although closer to Bruce Springsteen than Billy Bragg.

Monsour’s music is inscribed with activism. He is a founder and coordinator of Justice for Palestine Magan-djin, the Palestinian solidarity organisation that, since October 2023, has spearheaded the movement in Magan-djin, organising hundreds of rallies, pickets, vigils and public meetings. The size and intensity of this mobilisation has surpassed anything before it in the city’s history, including the struggle against the United States war in Vietnam.

Monsour composes and sings as a partisan of this uprising, a musician-activist, rather than a musician-ally. Without ever assuming to speak for Palestinians, some of his songs on Time of Monsters adopt a Palestinian first-person perspective. “Free Me from the Dust”, for example, addresses the horror in Gaza from the viewpoint of a Palestinian survivor: “In this shroud I bury soon something inside of me, flesh that binds me.” In “One Day in the Sun”, Monsour describes a Gazan’s daily struggle for survival: “All I can do is breathe, all I can do is wait, wait for tomorrow, and one day in the sun.” In another track, “I Am Not a Number”, the narrator tells us, “I live beyond your pictures; this land and I, we are the same.”

The Palestinian persona of these songs, however, is not ubiquitous across the album. The lens of the title song cuts away to an ally watching the genocide in livestream: “I am staring at something, can’t look away, the past the future is haunting me this day, crimes that echo on a million screens.”

The effect of this shifting perspective from song to song is a reframing of the Palestinian “I” as a “we” of the global liberation movement, positioning the Palestinians as a universal subject and Monsour himself (and us) as part of that multitude. “Our world is in pieces,” he declares in “Long List of Lost Things”, speaking for all of us. Monsour’s own place in the struggle — his own authorial “I” — is never far from the surface: “I can’t say if I’m broken, I can’t say if I’m whole, I just keep walking, nowhere else to go.”

This positioning gives the lyrical content of Time of Monsters urgency and emotional immediacy that sets Monsour’s songwriting apart in the genre of protest music. Woody Guthrie, Pete Seeger and Joan Baez, to name just three of the luminaries in the political folk tradition, sang about the resistance of the oppressed, often joining them in song at picket lines and rallies.

Even Bob Dylan, in his early years, occasionally engaged directly with the subjects of his protest tunes. Today, the likes of Macklemore, Roger Waters and Irish rappers Kneecap sing in solidarity with the Palestinians, using their profiles to mainstream the cause and call out the complicity of so-called non-alignment.

Monsour occupies a different place in this tradition. His songs not only articulate the demands for liberation, they are infused with the temper of the liberation movement itself. They do not constitute — to invoke an old cliché — the “soundtrack” of a movement. They are not an appendage. They are the resistance talking to itself and the world at large in verse and chorus, guitar in hand, amp turned up. They register the intensity of the rally, the march, the picket. They stridently declaim justice, urging everyone to keep showing up, to fight the despair with active solidarity, to believe that the monsters of our time can be vanquished by our collective efforts.

And as these monsters keep going about their awful business, these songs also speak to our grief and doubt. “Can we repair what is broken, rebuild what is left?”, we are asked.

The pedigree of such resistance art can be found in the activist songs of the Industrial Workers of the World, in “Bella Ciao” and the European anti-fascists, in the African American spirituals transformed into anthems of perseverance by the underground, and of course in the poetry of Palestinians themselves.

It is a tradition with a deeply personal dimension. Monsour enacts resistance through his music, and that resistance is psychological as much as political. Confronting monstrous evil, this work of songwriting and performing serves as a metaphorical call to arms and an outlet for anguish.

This is art as politics and catharsis. And in both realms it lifts us up, prepares us to struggle another day, one step closer to liberation. “Revolution love will see us through,” Monsour assures us. In the end, Grendel was defeated by the warrior Beowulf. In Time of Monsters, Beowulf is all of us.

title: Accessible tram stop campaigners try to board Sydney Road tram
content:
After being ignored by the Victorian government for three-and-a-half years, the Sydney Road Accessible Tram Stops (SATS) campaign held an action on October 23.

A group of about 30 people, with and without mobility aids, attempted to board a tram on Sydney Road to highlight the inaccessibility.

While Sydney Road has many different classes of trams that run along it, campaigners waited for a low floor tram because it is those that would be accessible if tram stops were upgraded.

These could be used by people with mobility aids such as wheelchairs, walkers and crutches, but also by people with prams and shopping trolleys.

The rally waited for more than 20 minutes for a low floor tram to approach. Once it arrived, campaigners tried to board.

Protesters sang and chanted as they unsuccessfully attempted to board the tram.

One person had come with a ramp, and pointed out that the only way someone with a mobility issue could use a tram is to carry around a heavy ramp with them.
