author: Alfons Bech, Dick Nichols
title: International convoy seeks to boost solidarity with Ukraine from the bottom up
content:
Alfons Bech is the International Network for Solidarity with Ukraine (INSU) trade union coordinator and a member of the Coordination Group of the International Solidarity Convoy to Ukraine, organising its southern route from Barcelona to Kyiv.

Green Left’s Dick Nichols spoke to Bech about the convoy’s goals and organisation.

Where did the idea of the convoy come from?

It emerged on the second anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion [February 22, 2024], when the European Network for Solidarity with Ukraine (ENSU, now INSU) proposed organising a large international delegation of trade unionists to an event in Kyiv that the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine (FPU) and the Confederation of Free Trade Unions of Ukraine prepared with the support of the European Trade Union Confederation.

Trade unions participated in very large numbers, but online. Only one delegation went to Kyiv, representing the Catalan affiliate of the all-Spanish General Union of Workers (UGT).

The UGT delegation was very shocked by what they saw, but very pleased to have been there in person. They saw the devastation Russia had caused in Bucha and in the neighbourhoods of Kyiv, took part in the distribution of some material aid and got to know a little about Ukrainian culture.

From this, a sort of twinning has developed between the UGT and Ukrainian trade unions, which has been key to our understanding of this war and to the aid effort for Ukraine in Catalonia.

Many aid convoys have already gone to Ukraine. What makes this one different?

This convoy is building on what has already been done at the grassroots level in terms of aid to Ukraine. Nonetheless, this convoy takes place at a crucial moment for Ukraine and Europe.

We are entering the fifth year of a brutal war, and it is not clear how much further attacks the country’s already heavily damaged infrastructure can withstand.

The experience of the past four years shows Ukrainian workers will continue to suffer greatly from always having to repair infrastructure under enemy fire. Russia, conscious of this situation, is preparing to attack even more forcefully what is essential to the survival of the population: energy, cities, hospitals, schools, the bridges of Kyiv, the water supply and the sewerage system

It is a genocidal plan. But it is not being implemented because Russia is doing well in the war or economically. [Vladimir] Putin’s regime faces many difficulties, and these are translating into savage attacks on Ukraine’s civilian population and more repression within Russia.

In this situation of extreme need, we know that any help the convoy can provide, while useful, will be a drop in the ocean.

That is one potent reason why the convoy must have an extra, political, dimension, as a public and visible show of support from the working people of the rest of Europe to their sisters and brothers in Ukraine.

It repeats the cry of the Spanish Civil War, ¡No Pasaran! (They shall not pass) against today’s enemies of human and democratic rights and their chief guarantor, the majority of working people.

We, in Catalonia, cannot bear to see in Ukraine a repeat of the Spanish Republic’s fate, which was abandoned in the face of international fascism. That treachery by great “civilised” powers intent on appeasing [Adolf] Hitler and [Benito] Mussolini cost the peoples of the Spanish state forty years of fascism.

So, the stakes could not be higher…

It is why we in INSU see the need for the sort of sharp expansion of solidarity action that the convoy represents — it is not enough for us to just carry on doing what we have been doing up to now.

What the convoy offers is not only humanitarian or material aid. It is also an instrument for showing that boosted solidarity with Ukraine starts from the bottom up.

This is not just a message about getting more and bigger donations, but of raising awareness about what the overall effort of solidarity with Ukraine must involve.

One critically important example: it is urgent Ukraine receive the €210 billion in frozen Russian assets held by Western financial institutions, such as Euroclear, to fund its defence effort.

While most European governments are looking for ways to cut social spending and increase military spending, these same governments are reluctant to declare the kind of financial war on the Kremlin that would be involved in releasing these assets to Ukraine.

The convoy will be a platform for this and other important messages.

What organisations are supporting the convoy?

As of early October, a growing number of trade union organisations, social movements and elected representatives from 20 countries have officially supported the convoy.

Trade union support includes the FPU, the Swiss Trade Union Federation, the Brazilian Trade Union and Popular Centre Conlutas, the General Labour Federation of Belgium, the Belgian Confederation of Christian Trade Unions, the UGT of Catalonia, the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation, the University and College Union of the United Kingdom and the Theatre and Performing Arts Trade Union of Norway.

It is also supported by more than 20 political organisations and parties spanning Europe, the Americas, Asia and Oceania, and more than 40 MPs and public representatives, including 18 Members of the European Parliament.

More than 50 solidarity associations, NGOs and independent media outlets have also expressed support. All of this can be found on the convoy’s website, which we update weekly as the number of organisations and volunteers grows.

The convoy has launched its own fund appeal. Where is it at?

The convoy’s central fund appeal “Generators and Stoves to Ukraine” is now [October 19] approaching 30% of its €100,000 target, after a bit more than a month of serious effort.

This shows the initiative is reaching a broader audience of people who want to do something for Ukraine.

What is the convoy planning to take to Ukraine?

The main “cargo” will be generators, wood-burning stoves, medical supplies, electrical equipment that cannot be sourced in Ukraine and vehicles.

We will provide humanitarian aid, supplying whatever we can of the requests received from Ukrainian organisations.

What impact, if any, do you expect the convoy to have inside Ukraine?

The convoy, while supporting Ukraine’s rights and its resistance in general, also looks to help strengthen trade unions and civil society organisations inside Ukraine and make them more visible in the rest of Europe.

That is why we stand with workers’ unions, student unions, nurses’ unions and railway unions when the Ukrainian government attacks their rights.

We hope the arrival of the convoy will demonstrate that there is support from workers in the rest of Europe for Ukrainian workers and trade unions.

Can solidarity with Palestine go with solidarity with Ukraine?

The convoy does not require participants to take a position on Palestine, but my personal response is: “Yes, it should.” Both peoples are victims of ruthless attacks by aggressive colonialist powers that want to lay hold of their wealth and, moreover, root out their very culture.

The key difference is that Ukraine has a real state while Palestine does not. That is why Ukraine can defend itself much better than the Palestinians. But the underlying problem, which is the right to self-determination of nations, is identical.

By being passive or indifferent about either oppressed nation, you effectively offer support to their oppressor. That is why we in INSU go to demonstrations for both Ukraine and Palestine with a banner that says: “From Ukraine to Palestine, occupation is a crime.”

What final message would you give to anyone reading this interview? Why should they support this convoy?

This convoy is an opportunity for everyone who wants to do something to end a horrendously cruel invasion on just terms.

For everyone who has no trouble recognising that this aggression was started by Putin, not NATO, and who want to do something to support Ukrainians’ just resistance.

For everyone who does not want to be on the wrong side of history or have their conscience scarred by the thought of having done nothing until the war was over.

author: Paul Gregoire
title: Allega Spender pushes to remove religious exemptions against LGBTIQ students, teachers
content:
The Sex Discrimination and Fair Work Amendment (Equality in Treatment in Religious Schools) Bill 2026, introduced on October 12, seeks to repeal the offending exemptions in federal sex discrimination law as well as removing the related provisions in federal workplace relations law. It also extends protections to associates of those who are captured under the current exemptions.

Section 38 of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (SDA) makes it lawful for religious education institutions to discriminate against a teacher, student or contract worker due to their “sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, marital or relationship status or pregnancy”.

The proposal took centre stage in 2018, as the national religious freedoms debate took off prior to then-Coalition Prime Minister Scott Morrison shooting it down.

Morrison’s push to establish a religious freedoms regime in 2018 uncovered their existence. His years-long religious crusade was defeated after debate on these exemptions.

Labor PM Anthony Albanese promised to progress the reform in 2022, but changed his mind.

Spender, independent MP for Wentworth, is pushing popular reforms, despite far-right commentators claiming it as an attack on religious freedom.

“These exemptions have already been removed in state and territory law, to varying degrees, but there are no national standards,” Spender told NSW Parliament on October 12.

“The Australian Law Reform Commission’s 2024 review found that religious schools could still maintain their ethos without this exemption.

“At its heart, section 38 of the Sex Discrimination Act is repealed in its entirety and replaced with a far narrower provision,” Spender said in her second reading speech on her private member’s bill.

“Protections are also extended to a person’s associates ... This means a child cannot be treated differently just because she has two mums.”

The bill repeals the current provisions affecting students, teachers and contract workers in section 38, replacing it with a provision that allows institutions to preference staff based on faith in two ways — at their initial employment and in the promotion of senior leadership roles such as “principal, vice-principal, religious education teacher, chaplain” or any other comparable role.

The bill inserts section 7AAA into the SDA, which makes it unlawful to discriminate against an associate, such as a spouse or relative, of a person protected under the Act. It removes provisions that permitted discrimination based on sex, sexuality or gender.

It also repeals provisions in the Fair Work Act 2009 that extend discrimination into workplace agreements.

“But preferencing is not a licence to discriminate,” Spender said. “A school can choose a candidate because of their faith. It cannot fire someone because of their sexuality. Many students have wonderful, formative experiences at religious schools. Many LGBTQIA+ students come out to their friends and teachers in these schools and are accepted. But … this is not everyone’s experience.”

The exemptions in section 38 of the SDA relating to sexual orientation and gender identity, were inserted into the Act when a 2013 bill added anti-discrimination provisions into the law that related to sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics. The exemptions in respect of gay and transgender individuals joined pre-existing ones that permitted discrimination based on sex.

The October 2018 Ruddock review into religious freedoms recommended tightening these exemptions in federal law, which drew attention to and then condemnation of the laws.

While Morrison initially tried to downplay the outcry, he reversed course and promised to repeal the discriminatory measures targeting students. But Morrison, a Pentecostal, attempted to progress three versions of the Religious Freedoms Bill — two in 2019 and one in 2022 — and the removal of any exemptions was forgotten.

Each version of the religious freedoms legislation was increasingly watered down.

Three years of debate on these laws made it clear that his measures sought religious privileges.

The public debate over religious concerns is different to the present, with the conservative push to insert the controversial International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism into all levels of government to curb criticism of Israel and its genocide.

At the beginning of the decade, arch-conservative Christians were pushing to ensure that their religious beliefs trumped everyone else’s. The five-year-long religious freedoms debate came to an abrupt end in early 2022 when Morrison shelved the bill at the eleventh hour.

This was because five Liberal MPs crossed the floor to support an amendment by independent MP Rebekha Sharkie, which sought to make it unlawful to expel gay and trans students. Morrison was not prepared to allow this change for trans students.

Albanese promised to remove exemptions for students and teachers in the lead-up to the May 2022 election.

In March 2024, Labor had two draft laws — one to remove the exemptions and the other to progress religious discrimination protections. But as it did not receive Coalition support, both were dropped.

Spender told parliament that since 2016 there have been ten inquiries, more than 260 hearings and more than 70,000 submissions related to religious discrimination and the removal of the exemptions. She questioned why four years after federal Labor made a commitment, nothing had been done.

She said that while the removal of the exemptions will not encroach on the way in which religious educational institutions operate for the most part, the repeal of the law is necessary because, as it stands, the message it sends rings out “well beyond the school gate”. The existing laws say that discrimination against LGBTIQ people is permitted on some occasions.

“Australians expect equality in front of the law, not least from those institutions that are partly funded by taxpayers,” Spender added. “Getting this balance right is not easy, but our laws need to be applied fairly across our country. I think there is a practical and sensible pathway through this … that this parliament could unite around.”

[Paul Gregoire writes for Sydney Criminal Lawyers where this piece was first published.]

author: Ben Radford
title: US must end its cruel blockade of Cuba
content:
Every year since 1992, the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has overwhelmingly voted to end the United States government’s cruel and illegal economic blockade of Cuba. One-hundred-and-sixty-five countries voted last year for the resolution on the “Necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba”, with just six against.

This year’s vote, on October 28, takes place as escalating US economic warfare against Cuba is causing a devastating humanitarian crisis. The blockade’s impacts have been characterised as a “silent genocide”, severely restricting Cubans’ access to food, medicine, equipment and fuel, and impacting every aspect of daily life.

The Cuban government submitted its annual report to the UNGA in September, detailing last year’s impacts of the US blockade. Between March last year and February this year, the blockade inflicted more than US$8 billion worth of damages.

The economic cost of just four days of the blockade amounts to the cost of all fuel imports needed to meet Cuba’s demand.

On top of existing strangulation mechanisms, the US government imposed an energy blockade on Cuba in January, claiming that the country posed an “unusual and extraordinary threat” to US national security.

The US announced tariffs on goods from countries that, directly or indirectly, sold or provided oil to Cuba. Following the US’s January 3 attacks on Venezuela, it also blocked all Venezuelan oil shipments to the country.

The energy blockade is the reason for widespread blackouts, as well disruptions to water supply, waste collection and transport.

The fuel shortages are severely impacting hospital operations, including treatments that require a steady energy supply, such as haemodialysis. There are harrowing reports of surgeons having to perform operations by mobile phone lights, due to the blackouts.

The US blockade has affected Cubans’ access to vital treatment and medicine. One example is Cuba’s cancer survival rates, which, while still higher than many low- and middle-income countries, have dropped from 85% to 65%.

Cuba’s infant mortality has risen from 4 out of 1000 live births in 2018 to 9.9 last year — a 148% rise.

Cuban authorities say that the current transport crisis is more acute than during the “Special Period” in the 1990s following the collapse of the Soviet Union, which plunged Cuba into a prolonged economic crisis. Fuel shortages have affected refrigerated transport, preventing more than 30,000 children from receiving vaccines.

In May, the US imposed a regime of secondary sanctions against governments and companies that invest in or trade with Cuba.

For example, the US Office of Foreign Assets Control has imposed fines on US companies for handling cargo shipments bound for Cuba and providing services for people living in the country.

Over the past year, 34 international banking institutions suspended or declined to conduct operations with Cuba, citing risks of secondary sanctions.

Several airlines have ceased operations in Cuba and many international hotel chains also abandoned management agreements for hotels, citing the risks posed by the secondary sanctions regime. These sanctions — along with other US measures — have contributed to the collapse in Cuba’s tourism industry.

“The application of these measures has produced a sophisticated mechanism of asphyxiation directed at the Cuban population, exceeding by far the levels of pressure historically imposed over decades,” the annual report said.

It also notes that the blockade has caused US$3.9 trillion worth of damages since it was imposed. However, it said the impacts go far beyond economic losses, causing suffering, illness and death.

The US blockade of Cuba violates not just international law, but any semblance of humanity.

The US government has made its intention of achieving “regime change” in Cuba by the end of the year very clear; it is openly considering the possibility of military attacks. This has been the US’s policy since Cubans overthrew the US-backed Fulgencio Batista military dictatorship in 1959 and set about implementing a planned economy based on meeting people’s needs.

Since then, the US has undertaken or sponsored terrorist attacks, a military invasion and an economic blockade against the Cuban people, with the explicit aim of bringing about “hunger, desperation and overthrow of government”, as revealed by a 1960 US memorandum.

The Cuban Embassy in Australia told Green Left that despite the challenges facing Cuba, it “remains committed to its social development and international cooperation”.

It noted that the Australian government voted in favour of last year’s UNGA resolution, calling for an end to the US blockade on Cuba.

The embassy encouraged the Labor government to engage in “constructive dialogue and to explore practical avenues of cooperation with Cuba in areas such as health, education, disaster resilience, renewable energy and scientific research”.

“At a time when the world faces complex economic, environmental and humanitarian challenges, greater engagement and cooperation with Cuba, rather than continued sanctions, would benefit both the Cuban people and the international community.”

Since 1963, Cuba has sent more than 600,000 health professionals overseas to provide care and train personnel, mostly in low-income regions. The US aims to destroy Cuba’s model of medical internationalism, pressuring countries to terminate often decades-long Cuban medical missions.

More than 160 countries have benefited from Cuba’s medical internationalism, including its pandemic and disaster response to free training for tens of thousands of medical personnel.

The embassy also said that it “deeply appreciates” the Australian solidarity movement with Cuba, saying it has “demonstrated a steadfast commitment to friendship and cooperation between our peoples” over many years.

“Through educational activities, public advocacy, cultural exchanges and community engagement, solidarity organisations and supporters across Australia have played a valuable role in raising awareness about the impact of the blockade and in promoting closer people-to-people ties.

“The annual vote at the United Nations is an important reminder of the overwhelming international rejection of the blockade and the need for policies that promote development, mutual respect and people-to-people exchange.”

United Nations General Assembly

HJA singled out the Australian Manufacturing Workers’ Union for “critical political and strategic support in advancing the proposal”, as well as Hunter Renewal, which championed this reform long before HJA’s involvement.

The only way to guarantee that working-class communities’ rights are safeguarded is by electing socialists who are also committed community activists.

title: Residents rally against Inner West Council’s pro-developer plan
content:
About 300 people rallied outside the Inner West Council meeting at Ashfield Town Hall on October 20 to demand real consultation time and more information about its so-called Fairer Future Plan 2 (FFP2).

The Fairer Future Part 1’s rezoned large sections of the inner west for luxury high-rise apartments.

The rally was organised by No High Rise Lilyfield and supported by a range of community groups, including the Better Future Coalition, Leichhardt Matters, Save Marrickville, Save Dulwich Hill and Action for Public Housing.

Lucy Wynter from No High Rise Lilyfield said the Fairer Future plan is “ill-conceived, underdone, under-prepared, not explained to the public and the time we’ve had to digest it has been paltry”.

Wynter said that when FFP2 was announced, she started a WhatsApp group chat with neighbours and friends in Lilyfield. A few weeks later, there are 700 members of the group chat, “about 10% of the population of Lilyfield. That shows how much this matters to people.”

Lilyfield residents did not receive a notice about FFP2 until two weeks into the six-week consultation period and many have still not received any information at all.

title: Socialist Alliance: ‘Stop weaponising shocking attack on Helen Haines MP’
content:
Socialist Alliance condemns the terrible attack on Helen Haines MP and we send our best wishes to her and her family.

This shocking incident had been politically weaponised even before the facts were established; the corporate media and some MPs went looking to find someone to blame.

The Zionists and right-wing commentators were quick to blame the pro-Palestine movement, because the alleged perpetrator — along with the majority of people in Australia — was critical of Israel’s genocide in Gaza. It has become stock in trade for mainstream media to brand critics of Israel as “extremist”.

We now know the alleged perpetrator suffered from poor mental health and that their family was friends with the Haines family.

As pressures mount around housing affordability and the rising cost of living, poorly resourced mental health services, especially in regional and rural Victoria, may contribute to anti-social behaviour.

The 2021 Royal Commission into Victoria’s Mental Health System made 65 recommendations and nine interim recommendations. These largely remain unfunded or not implemented, despite the Victorian Labor government promising to do so.

author: Peter Boyle
title: Why the billionaire class has to go
content:
One of the saddest aspects about the global wave of right-wing populism is how many people are in awe of the billionaires who are literally destroying our future.

Back in the age of feudal despots, lavish palaces, pomp and ceremony, the superstitious belief in the “divine right” of the rulers to rule helped keep the masses in line.

While many of those old superstitions have worn thin, they have been replaced by the myth that the mega rich are where they are because they have brilliant minds, or have worked their way to the top.

But this myth is also wearing thinner — thanks to United States President Donald Trump’s narcissistic outbursts and the obscene growth in the wealth of the mega rich.

All that remains in the billionaire’s ideological armoury is their capacity to fund the spread of more racism, misogyny, hate and bigotry.

Hence Trump’s toxic bullying and the blatant white supremacy propagated by Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, through his social media platform X (formerly Twitter).

The sheer amount of wealth the billionaire class has accumulated refutes the lie that it was earned through hard work. Oxfam estimates their combined wealth at $18.3 trillion.

This year, Musk became the first trillionaire.

If a worker somehow managed to save $50,000 a year, it would take 20 million years to get to a trillion dollars.

title: Is France burning down? The French revolt, rioting and the radical left
content:
Rioting is the voice of the unheard, and is completely inevitable once a spark of revolt arrives after months and years of austerity, extreme police violence and racism. Of course that doesn't mean the job of anticapitalists is to make plans about what buildings to burn next week. We don't want our young people to end up in prison for decades! The more organised and effective collective action is at all levels, the less chaos there will be, anyway. Union leaders need to build mass strikes quickly.

“Now that the focus is on all this violence, can you really recommend that school kids continue going to demonstrations?” asked a slimy journalist on France Info, the national 24-hour news radio, of a young activist, the morning after Saturday’s [October 17] day of action. Meanwhile Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, whose public relations team had been up all night racking their brains, managed nothing more sophisticated than to blame the unrest across the country on the radical left France Insoumise (France in Revolt).

Eight hundred thousand people joined demonstrations in dozens of towns on October 17. The protests were characterised by an explosion of popular creativity and anger. title: The climate-changing policy behind Türkiye’s floods
content:
On October 14, a 14-year-old boy stepped into a puddle in a park in Balat, in Istanbul’s old city, and was electrocuted. A surveillance camera captured the moment. The governor’s office has opened an investigation.

The same storms flooded five other provinces, including Antalya, which will be host to COP31 in less than four weeks.

Istanbul alone recorded 1277 floods and 15 landslides; schools closed the next day.

None of this was a surprise. The day before the state meteorological service forecast about 21–50 millimetres of rain for Istanbul; parts of the city’s north received nearly 194mm. Cities are meant to be built for the worst case scenario, not the forecast.

Was this climate change? Without an attribution study, it is too early to say, but we do not need one to explain what happened.

Istanbul is a city of concrete and asphalt. Over five years, 98 square kilometres of new floor space was completed and 124 square kilometres started; more than a million new cars joined the traffic.

If you could park every vehicle in the city nose to tail, you would have a 12–lane car park from Istanbul to Paris.

title: City of Sydney for Palestine joins calls for council to boycott Airbnb
content:
City of Sydney for Palestine is joining housing justice organisers to call on the City of Sydney Council to boycott Airbnb and support strong laws for short-stay rentals.

Airbnb is a target of the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement because of its role in enabling tourism in illegal Israeli settlements in the Occupied West Bank.

Airbnb helps normalise Israel’s occupation, apartheid and dispossession of Palestinians from their homeland by listing and profiting from accommodation on stolen Palestinian land.

Airbnb is helping turn occupied land into a tourism market. It is helping normalise dispossession. It is making money while Palestinians are denied freedom, safety and return.

Airbnb is also part of the housing crisis in Australia.

There is severe housing stress in the Sydney, where Rents are rising and vacancies are low. Meanwhile, thousands of homes are being used as short-term rentals through platforms like Airbnb.

Sydney’s vacancy rate was just 2.1%, according to the ABC in August, but there were 10,531 active Airbnb listings.

Airbnb and short-term rental platforms allow homes to be converted into commercial tourist accommodation, while renters are pushed further into crisis.

title: Do we really need AI mega data centres?
content:

There has been a lot of discussion about AI data centres being critical infrastructure. Do we need these mega AI data centres and what is the difference between cloud data centres and AI data centres?

There is no meaningful race that Australia or Victoria can be part of.

content:
More than 200 people attended the inaugural Dr Adnan Al-Bursh Memorial Lecture on October 17, hosted by Australian Healthcare Alliance for Palestine and Nurses and Midwives for Palestine.

The lecture aims to pay tribute to those who use their knowledge and expertise to demand human dignity, justice and freedom.

Al-Bursh, a prominent Palestinian orthopaedic surgeon and head of orthopaedics at Al-Shifa Hospital in the Gaza Strip, was born on September 17, 1974. He was tortured to death at the Ofer Prison in the Occupied West Bank and died on April 19, 2024 — just 50 years of age.

A striking image of Al-Bursh, by Mandy King, was displayed at the front of the meeting.

content:

content:

content:

Gulfer Olan, co-chair of the Federation of Democratic Kurdish Society Australia, said this was “an historical milestone”.

Boyd explained that it took seven years and the hard work of many people to get to the Parliamentary Friends of the Kurdish People officially established. “I resonate with the spirit of the Kurdish community, your commitment to grassroots democracy, your commitment to gender equality and economic equality, your love of nature, the environment.”

D’Adam said: “We are one in commitment to democracy and human rights, the right to self-determination and the right to cultural autonomy... [this is] another marker of the status that this community now holds in Australian society as an important part of our multicultural community.”

title: In Gaza, even thinking has become a struggle
content:
I have thought carefully about how to write about my life in Gaza. Even speaking about what we experience requires caution. How can I tell the truth about my reality without putting myself at risk?

This question alone says something about what it means to live here.

My days have become a series of moments. in which survival takes priority over everything else.

At night, the sound of surveillance drones makes it difficult to think about anything beyond the possibility that we could be next. Even when the sky grows quiet, peace feels unreal. At night, closing my eyes no longer feels different from opening them.

Our homes are destroyed, yet we still hope to recover even one small belonging from the rubble.

We want something to carry from our past into a future we cannot imagine.

Sometimes, the movement of rats among the ruins makes us wonder whether danger has returned. Even animals seek shelter in the remains of our homes, while we cannot safely retrieve the things that once made those homes ours.

Then comes the daily search for drinking water.

In 2026, finding clean water should not be the greatest problem occupying a person's mind. Yet we wait in line, hoping to receive enough to get through the day. title: ‘Wall of Tears’ memorialises Gaza’s lost children
content:
The Wall of Tears exhibition, memorialising the 18,500 children officially recorded as killed by Israeli forces over two years in Gaza from October 7, 2023, opened at the Pitt Street Uniting Church, in Sydney, on October 9.

The exhibition is supported by Amnesty International Australia (AIA) and Palestinian Christians in Australia. The 15-metre-long artwork is on loan from Perth Doctors Medical Aid for Palestine and is open to the public until October 28.

The Wall of Tears lists the names of children killed in Gaza between October 7, 2023, and July 19, 2025, alongside photographs and stories.

Barbara Gorman, convenor of AIA's Pennant Hills Action Group, told Green Left that the exhibition “confronts us with the human reality behind the devastating number of children killed in Gaza. Every name on this Wall represents a child, a life, a family and a future.

“We hope that by bringing the Wall to Sydney, people will take the time to see those names, reflect on the scale of this loss and remember the children behind the numbers.”

Created by United States artist Phil Buehler, the Wall was first displayed in Brooklyn, New York, in January. A replica was later brought to Australia and has been displayed in Western Australia and on the lawns of Parliament House in Canberra.

This is about 65 times larger than the 6800 people believed to be dead or missing from the recent Nepal flash flood. title: Why the RBA wants higher unemployment
content:
The latest official unemployment rate was released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on September 24. It was 4.6% in August, seasonally adjusted, up from 4.2% a year ago. By its calculations, the number of unemployed people had grown by 12.4% in that period to 722,900. Another 6.3% were underemployed.

Two days earlier, Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Governor Michele Bullock took part in a “Fireside Chat at the Committee for Economic Development of Australia”, where she revealed that this was on the lower end of the RBA’s unemployment target of between 4.5% and 5%.

Higher unemployment, she said, will take the “heat out of the labor market” and “ease pressure on inflation”.

Every RBA governor swears blind that everything the RBA does is to “fight inflation”. If some people get hurt in the process, sorry, that is just a necessary sacrifice because inflation hurts everyone.

However, the RBA governor admitted that inflation “really hits the most vulnerable in the community the hardest”.

“They’re the ones that have the least ability and income to move ... They have less flexibility. They have less discretionary expenditure ... So inflation really, really hits the people on the lowest incomes the hardest.”

So is the RBA getting on the side of the poorest?

In Ireland, a wave of far-right protests in 2022 targeting refugee and asylum-seeker accommodation sites was followed by a racist riot in Dublin in November 2023, in the aftermath of a stabbing attack. content:

Friends of Pine Creek (FoPC) is campaigning to stop logging in a 1600-hectare area of PCSF, which provides the corridor between Bongil Bongil National Park and Bindarri National Park.

FoPC facilitator Susan Harwood told Green Left the group welcomed the NSW Labor government’s Great Koala National Park (GKNP) announcement, but said the proposed boundaries leave a crucial gap between two “intergenerationally significant areas” of koala habitat.

title: Lizzie O’Shea: ‘Surveillance technology is a threat to democracy’
content:
Lizzie O’Shea, a writer, lawyer and founder of Digital Rights Watch, told the New South Wales Council for Civil Liberties’ (NSWCCL) annual fundraising dinner and journalism awards on October 1 that rapidly developing surveillance technology is throwing up many challenges.

Digital technology and democracy are in a “significant amount of tension”, O’Shea said. She added that defending civil liberties is not about “clever people working to impose civil liberties on everybody else”, but that campaigners “have to convince a critical mass that they have to defend their own rights”.

Referencing the origins of professional policing in London in the late 18th century, she described it as “a period of immense technological disruption”, as the Industrial Revolution was reshaping society.

The new police force, O’Shea said, was used to “monitor, enforce and impose the new conditions of social order”. Specifically, it ensured merchants’ profits and prevented dockworkers from supplementing their wages by pilfering stock. The idea was to get the state and industry to collaborate, with a “form of surveillance of everyday people”.

“Policing was talked about as a new science in the detection and prevention of crime,” she said. The spectacle of force “offered an economical and effective way of maintaining order”.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: University of Sydney threatens to throttle student body for being pro-Palestine
content:
University of Sydney (USyd) management is pursuing its anti-democratic practices, with a threat to defund the main student representative body and take over its election process.

It comes as NSW Labor Premier Chris Minns and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese intervened in the recent Student Representative Council (SRC) elections, describing a pro-Palestine “Globalise the Intifada” ticket as antisemitic.

It appears that they lent on Usyd management, which is now threatening to defund and take over the SRC elections.

Honi Soit reported on September 28 that a source, “privy to proceedings of the University Senate”, said that Vice-Chancellor Mark Scott “raised the possibility of the university taking over responsibility for SRC elections”. It was an un-minuted segment of the meeting.

The recent SRC elections returned incumbent president Grace Street, who led the Grassroots ticket, which is also pro-Palestine. A referendum on the university cutting ties with Israel and weapons companies complicit in genocide was held at the same time and passed with about 90% of the vote.

Scott and Chancellor David Thodey released a statement claiming that the phrase “Globalise the intifada” is “hate speech” and “incit[es] violence”.

author: Sue Bull
title: Protesters tell Pauline Hanson she is unwelcome in Djilang, Ballarat
content:
“Migrants are welcome racists are not,” rang out as protesters gathered near the Beckley Markets as Pauline Hanson arrived for her $50-a-head BBQ on October 4.

The snap protest was organised by Geelong against Racism (GAR), which includes Geelong Trades Hall, Socialist Alliance and Geelong Anarchist Communists.

Tim Gooden, one of the organisers who from Socialist Alliance told Green Left he was happy with the turn given they did not know the venue until earlier that same day.

“Hanson’s people kept it secret as they are worried about opposition.” GAR organisers said the BBQ did not attract 200 people, as local media claimed, as only about 50 cars came in and many had a sole occupant.

Many local residents who attended the protest expressed their concerns about One Nation’s (ON) racist politics.

Sarah Hathway, the Socialist Alliance candidate for Corio, who regularly campaigns at the Beckley Markets, told Green Left she had heard more residents saying that they will vote for ON.

“These are working class people who feel desperate. They have been sold out by Labor and the Liberals and ON is promising that life will get better with fewer migrants. But I’m afraid ON is not the answer.”

author: Jim McIlroy
title: Snap protest demands Labor pressure US to stop its war on Cuba, Venezuela
content:
The Australia-Cuba Friendship Society (ACFS) and the Australia-Venezuela Solidarity Network (AVSN) called a snap rally on October 3 to demand the United States stop threatening and blockading Cuba, Venezuela and Latin America.

It was part of an international day, called by the US United National Anti-War Coalition, to defend the sovereignty of Latin America, particularly Cuba and Venezuela.

US peace organisation CODEPINK said on September 30 that it had information that the US Army Reserve was preparing to invade Cuba, in three to four months’ time. The US Southern Command is allegedly massing military police, engineers, medical units, battlefield surgical capacity and major logistics forces.

The rally demanded that the federal Labor federal government call on the US government to stop its invasion plans of Cuba and lift the 60-year blockade, and end the 10-year blockade on Venezuela.

It also called for Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and Cilia Flores’s release from the notorious US Federal Prison in Brooklyn, where they have imprisoned for eight months on trumped-up charges of drug trafficking.

Coral Wynter, from AVSN and Socialist Alliance (SA), told the rally: “All of Latin America is now under threat from a resurgence of the 19th century Monroe doctrine, with fascist-leaning, US-dominated puppet governments agreeing to US military bases and foreign interference.

author: Sarah Glynn
title: French lessons on authoritarianism and solidarity: The lycée student blockades
content:
For French lycée (high school) students, this week has been an important step in their education. You can study books about the role of the state and of the forces of law and order, of political deception and media bias, and of organisation and solidarity; but that is not the same as practical experience.

This week they learnt the meaning of authoritarianism, and that the official values of the French Republic — liberté, égalité, fraternité (liberty, equality, fraternity) — have to be fought for again and again. They have also provided a lesson in solidarity for us all.

As in other countries that have undergone years of neoliberal austerity, French schools suffer from chronic underfunding. This affects everything from teacher shortages to building maintenance, and is especially bad in poorer areas. The students have had enough of this undermining of their futures and are on strike.

They are protesting the lack of crucial teachers and other staff, large class sizes, overloaded timetables, badly maintained buildings, and the discriminatory system for allocating university places.

Their main form of action has been blockades of their lycées, supplemented by spontaneous marches and supported by general assemblies.

author: Igor Ojeda
title: Brazil’s elections and environmental policy: A choice between continuity and dismantling
content:
Never before in the history of this country has the climate crisis been as relevant to a presidential election as it, very likely, will be in the 2026 vote. Once again deeply polarised, this year’s electoral contest between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers’ Party and Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party is taking place against a decisive climatic and geopolitical backdrop.

Less than a year ago, in November 2025, Brazil hosted the United Nations’ annual climate summit, COP, that restored the country’s status as a key player in the global climate debate. This was a particularly important development given that Brazil currently ranks among the top five contributors to greenhouse gas emissions, primarily due to agriculture, cattle ranching and deforestation.

Four years after the last Brazilian presidential election, in which Lula defeated Jair Bolsonaro by a razor-thin margin, the effects of the climate crisis have intensified. As scientists and environmental, social and civil society organisations have been warning for years, the planet is increasingly suffering the severe consequences of this reality, with a rise in the frequency and intensity of extreme natural events, in addition to the increase in average global temperatures. author: Paul Gregoire
title: NSW extends youth bail crackdown, despite reduction in youth crime
content:
The Chris Minns Labor government wants to extend its 2024 youth bail crackdown in regional New South Wales, saying on September 15 it will remove the sunset clause to a law targeting 14- to 17-year-olds who have been charged with a serious motor theft or break and enter crimes and are on conditional release.

NSW Labor announced its “crack down” on young people in 2024 as Victoria, the Northern Territory and Queensland were rolling out similar laws.

The Justice Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous) Bill (No 2) 2026, introduced on September 15, includes an amendment to section 22C of the Bail Act 2013 (NSW) which removes the October 1 sunset clause. It will be extended until April 4, 2028.

The Aboriginal Legal Service NSW/ACT (ALS) criticised the move as discriminatory as it targets First Nations youth and “will only entrench them in a cycle of crime and disadvantage”.

author: Freya Hedley
title: One Nation doesn’t offer young or trans people a future
content:
The public’s distrust of the two parties, and the system in general, has become more pronounced over the last five years. Neither Labor or the Coalition have done anything to allay people’s fears, instead adopting some of One Nation’s (ON) policies.

Working class people’s lives have gotten harder, because wages have stagnated and the prices of basic goods and housing have continue to rise. People’s shopping baskets are lighter, but costing more.

Most young people have only experienced low wages and the loss of services.

People are scared, but also pissed off. This mood was palpable during COVID-19, but it never really went away after the pandemic restrictions lifted.

We are scared for our futures in a chaotic world, where governments wage continuous wars, and the climate emergency is getting worse.

The institutions people once believed in have betrayed them.

When people are in a state of constant anxiety, they look for the easiest answer.

That’s a factor in why ON won the by-election of the historically safe Labor seat of Secret Harbour in Western Australia.

But while ON likes to portray itself as a “protest” party — against the two major parties — its policies are just as pro-capitalist. Billionaire Gina Rinehart’s donation of a $2 million plane to Pauline Hanson and the Murdoch media’s adoration of ON makes that pretty clear.

title: Malaysia deports 1476 refugees to Myanmar
content:
There was outrage from refugee and human rights groups when Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced in July that his government had made an agreement with the military coup regime in Myanmar to deport 5000 Rohingya refugees who fled the regime's genocidal attacks on this Muslim minority.

The United Nations High Commission for Refugees (UNHCR) has registered 126,000 Rohingya refugees in Malaysia and there are more unregistered. Over the past year, these refugees have been targeted in a campaign of hate by figures in the conservative United Malays National Organisation, a component of the coalition federal government in Malaysia.

Green Left's Peter Boyle spoke to Madhavi Madhu, a member of the Socialist Party of Malaysia (PSM) and a longstanding refugee rights activist.

There have been reports that the Malaysian government has begun its promised deportations of refugees back to Myanmar. What is the actual situation?

The government deported 1476 Myanmar nationals (including women and children) on September 29 aboard two navy vessels and a hospital vessel. These individuals were detainees from various immigration detention camps. Large numbers of refugees remain in these detention facilities following continuous, large-scale raids that have taken place throughout this year.

author: Craig Brittain
title: The story of the League of Revolutionary Black Workers
content:
Motown and the making of working-class revolutionaries: The story of the League of Revolutionary Black Workers By Jerome Scott and Walda Katz-Fishman University of Georgia Press. 2025

Of all the radical groups to emerge in the United States in the 1960s, one of the most interesting was the League of Revolutionary Black Workers, which began organising in the car industry in Detroit, Michigan.

Jerome Scott and Walda Katz-Fishman’s book, Motown and the making of working-class revolutionaries, is based on extensive interviews with the surviving members of the league.

Before and after World War II, large numbers of African Americans moved north from the southern states to escape segregation and police violence, and in search of the $5-a-day industrialist Henry Ford was promising in his car factories. They were used to earning about $6 a week.

However, what they discovered in the car plants was that white workers got the pick of the jobs and Black workers did the dirty work. Management was white and so was the union. Both were racist.

Those who went north might not have experienced the legally sanctioned discrimination they’d experienced in the south, but there was plenty of discrimination nonetheless; in housing, education and employment. And the police were just the same.

author: Peter Boyle
title: Hunter Valley coal mine expansion approval bad for environment, jobs
content:
Steve O’Brien, the Socialist Alliance candidate for Newcastle in next year’s New South Wales election, said the September 30 decision of the NSW Independent Planning Commission to approve the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) Mine Continuation Project, the largest coal mine expansion ever proposed in NSW, was a very bad decision.

“It is bad for our Pacific neighbours, who are already feeling the effects of rising sea levels,” O’Brien told Green Left. “It is bad for our environment because it will worsen the bushfires, floods and other catastrophic climate events. And it’s also bad for workers.

“We’ve been told by the Chris Minns Labor government that 1500 jobs have been saved by this decision, but that figure needs to be seriously interrogated.

“Who really trusts Glencore, which owns these mines, to keep 1500 jobs until 2045?

“Glencore will continue to cut jobs — the number left when the mine eventually closes in 2045 will be a lot less than 1500.

“Glencore is in the business of making profits for its owners. In the capitalist system, that invariably means cutting jobs.”

O’Brien said that NSW Labor is being duplicitous, deliberately lying to working people about climate change and the serious challenge that it poses for this country.

title: Gen Z protests, Pax Silica and fighting for an ecosocialist future
content:
Khyl Ramos works on climate justice, labour rights and grassroots organising in the Philippines. He is the deputy project manager at Transform Asia Gender and Labor Institute and youth coordinator for the Party of the Labouring Masses (PLM).

Ramos was a guest speaker at the recent Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane, where he sat down with Green Left’s Ben Radford to discuss last year’s Gen Z protests, recent opposition to the United States-led Pax Silica initiative and the need for ecosocialist alternatives.

How would you characterise the Gen Z protests in the Philippines last year?

The Gen Z uprising in the Philippines last year was simultaneous with the protests in Indonesia, Nepal and Bangladesh.

title: 3 years of genocide rallies: Demand Labor cut ties with Israel
content:

Israel has murdered more than 1400 Gazans since the so-called “ceasefire” began in October last year. The genocide is still happening, albeit at a slower pace, because the United States is appeasing Israel. title: NSW Labor joins Qld Coalition’s defence of laws to silence criticism of genocide
content:

It signals that NSW plans to follow Queensland’s Liberal National Party government and enact its own law criminalising the expression “Globalise the intifada”.

JFP announced on July 28 it had launched a High Court challenge to Queensland’s so-called hate speech laws which prohibits the expression of the phrases “From the river to the sea” and “Globalise the intifada”. author: Lucy Millett
title: Students demand climate action in lead-up to COP31
content:
It has become abundantly clear that federal Labor’s net-zero deadlines mean nothing. Despite promising to act on the climate emergency, its approach to climate action are hollow threats of “reform” that enable coal and gas companies to continue profiting and growing.

In the lead-up to the COP31 summit, students are demanding better.

The net-zero initiative, which Labor has signed, commits it to reduce emissions 62-70% below 2005 levels by 2035, and achieve net-zero by 2050.

The Climate Council, among others, say this timescale to reduce polluting carbon emissions going into the atmosphere is not only not fast enough to limit the temperature rise to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels — as the 2015 Paris Agreement sets out.

But global climate pollution is not being cut fast enough and Australia is one of the main culprits.

The NSW Independent Planning Commission has just approved the Hunter Valley Operations Continuation Project on September 30, despite regional communities, including some in the industry, campaigning for sustainable jobs elsewhere.

Another 800 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions from this giant coal mine will contribute to the climate emergency.
